t: Napoleon wasn't short
p: The autopsy measured him at about 1.68 metres, average for his time. The report said “5 feet 2 inches”, but those were French units.
The myth grew from the shorter English inch, from British cartoons that drew him tiny, and from his soldiers' fond nickname, “le petit caporal”.
l: A misunderstood unit and a little propaganda are enough to create a myth that lasts two centuries.
q: Why do people think Napoleon was short?
French and English inches were confused
He said so in his memoirs

t: Cleopatra lived closer to us than to the pyramids
p: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, more than 2,500 years later.
Fewer than 2,000 years separate her from the Moon landing in 1969. To the Romans who conquered Egypt, the pyramids were already ancient history.
l: Antiquity is not one block: the ancients had their own distant past.
q: What is closer in time to Cleopatra?
The building of the Great Pyramid

t: Oxford is older than the Aztec capital
p: Teaching was already going on in Oxford in 1096. Tenochtitlán, the Aztec capital, was only founded in 1325, on an island in Lake Texcoco.
When the Spanish saw it in 1519, it was one of the largest cities in the world, and it was not yet two centuries old.
l: Civilisations we imagine as “ancient” can be younger than institutions that still exist.

t: The first university founded by a state
p: In 1224 Emperor Frederick II founded a Studium in Naples to train lawyers and officials for his kingdom.
Bologna and Paris had grown out of guilds of students and teachers, under the eye of the Church. Naples was created and funded by a ruler: the oldest state-run, secular university in the world.
l: Frederick II wanted skilled officials loyal to his kingdom, so he made his own university.
q: Who founded the University of Naples in 1224?

t: The ships that crossed a hill
p: An iron chain closed the Golden Horn and protected Constantinople from the sea. Sultan Mehmed II found a way around it.
He had about seventy ships dragged overland on greased logs, over the hill of Galata. Next morning the defenders found them in the harbour, behind their lines. The city fell on 29 May 1453.
l: When an obstacle looks impossible, sometimes the answer is to change the ground.
q: How did the Ottoman ships enter the Golden Horn?
They were dragged overland across a hill
They broke the chain with cannon fire
They slipped under the chain at night

t: The battle generals still study
p: In Apulia, Hannibal pushed his centre forward and let it fall back under Roman pressure. The legions marched straight into the pocket.
African infantry on the flanks and cavalry from behind closed them in on every side. In one afternoon Rome lost tens of thousands of men. It is the classic model of encirclement.
l: Giving way in the centre can win the battle on the flanks: the shape of a formation matters more than numbers.
q: What was Hannibal's key move at Cannae?
A siege of the Roman camp

t: There were more than 300 Spartans at Thermopylae
p: Leonidas' 300 fought alongside thousands of Greeks from many cities. When the Persians got round the pass by a mountain path, Leonidas sent most of the army away.
The Spartans stayed, with about 700 Thespians who refused to leave and 400 Thebans. Almost nobody remembers the Thespians.
l: Heroic stories simplify: behind “the 300” there are thousands of nameless people.
q: Who stayed with the Spartans to the end?

t: The ten days that never existed
p: The Julian calendar drifted by about 11 minutes a year. In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII fixed it with a clean cut.
In Italy, Spain and Portugal, Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October. Other countries switched much later: Britain in 1752, Russia in 1918.
l: Even time is a convention: to realign it with the Sun, Europe deleted ten days.
q: In Italy, which day followed Thursday 4 October 1582?

t: The October Revolution happened in November
p: In 1917 Russia still used the Julian calendar, 13 days behind the rest of Europe.

The storming of the Winter Palace took place on 25 October for Russians, but on 7 November by the Gregorian calendar. The Bolsheviks switched a few months later, and for decades the anniversary was celebrated in November.
l: An event can have two dates: it depends on the calendar of whoever tells the story.
q: What is the Gregorian date of the October Revolution?

t: Where the word “quarantine” comes from
p: During plague epidemics, in 1377 the Republic of Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, made arriving ships and travellers stay isolated for thirty days.
The period was later extended to forty, and from the Venetian “quaranta giorni”, forty days, came the word quarantine. The Black Death had just killed between a third and half of all Europeans.
l: Defences against epidemics are older than germ science: they came from observation.
q: How many days did Ragusa's first isolation last?

t: Vikings did not wear horned helmets
p: The only almost complete Viking helmet ever found, at Gjermundbu in Norway, is a simple iron cap with a guard for the eyes.
The horns arrived in 1876, with costumes designed by Carl Emil Doepler for Wagner's “Ring of the Nibelung”. In battle they would only have given the enemy something to grab.
l: Many “historical” images come from theatre and cinema, not from excavations.
q: Where does the image of horned Vikings come from?

t: In the Middle Ages they knew the Earth was round
p: Bede, Thomas Aquinas and the most widely used astronomy textbook in universities, Sacrobosco's “De sphaera”, all took a spherical Earth for granted.
The myth of a flat-Earth Middle Ages spread in the 1800s, helped by a fictional biography of Columbus written by Washington Irving in 1828.
l: The “dark and ignorant” Middle Ages is often an invention of later centuries.
q: What did medieval scholars think about the shape of the Earth?
That it was a floating disc

t: Columbus was wrong, his critics were right
p: The debate was not about the shape of the Earth but about its size. Columbus reckoned Japan was about 4,500 km from the Canaries: it is actually almost 20,000.
The experts who rejected his plan had better estimates. He was saved because, halfway there, lay a continent no one in Europe knew about.
l: Being right by luck is not being right: Columbus got his sums wrong and found a continent.
q: The position of the Canary Islands

t: Nero did not sing while Rome burned
p: According to Tacitus, when the great fire broke out Nero was in Antium. He returned to Rome, opened his gardens to the homeless and brought in cheap grain.
The rumour that he sang about the fall of Troy while watching the flames was already going round, but Tacitus reports it as gossip. Nero, for his part, blamed the fire on the Christians.
l: Rumours about a hated ruler outlive the facts.
q: Where was Nero when the fire broke out, according to Tacitus?

t: Pompeii may not have been destroyed in August
p: The traditional date, 24 August, comes from medieval copies of the letters of Pliny the Younger, who watched the eruption from Misenum.
But excavations have turned up pomegranates, chestnuts, lit braziers and, in 2018, a charcoal inscription dated to mid-October. Many scholars now favour 24 October.
l: A careless copyist can move a date for centuries: physical evidence corrects the texts.
q: Which clue points to an autumn eruption?
Traces of snow under the ash

t: The war began with a wrong turn
p: On 28 June 1914 a bomb thrown at Archduke Franz Ferdinand missed its target. Hours later his driver took a wrong turn, noticed the mistake and stopped to reverse.
Right there stood Gavrilo Princip, one of the conspirators, who fired from a few steps away. A month later Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.
l: Great crises have deep causes, but the moment they explode can depend on chance.
q: Why did the Archduke's car stop in front of Princip?
The driver had taken a wrong turn
It had run out of petrol
The crowd was blocking the street

t: The Christmas the war stopped
p: On Christmas Eve 1914, along parts of the Western Front, German and British soldiers sang carols from one trench to the other.
The next day they climbed out into no man's land: they swapped cigarettes, buried their dead and in some places played football. The commanders made sure it never happened again.
l: Even in the harshest war, an enemy seen up close becomes a person again.
q: What did some soldiers do in no man's land at Christmas 1914?

t: The “Byzantines” called themselves Romans
p: For a thousand years after the fall of Rome in the West, the Eastern Empire simply called itself the Roman Empire, and its people “Rhomaioi”, Romans, even though they spoke Greek.
The word “Byzantine” was made popular in 1557 by the German historian Hieronymus Wolf, more than a century after Constantinople fell.
l: The names we use to study the past are often not the ones its people used.
q: What did the people of the Eastern Empire call themselves?

t: Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire
p: That is how Voltaire dismissed the Holy Roman Empire in 1756. In theory it began with Charlemagne's coronation in 800.
By then it had become a patchwork of hundreds of principalities, free cities and bishoprics, with an elected emperor of limited power. It was dissolved in 1806, under pressure from Napoleon.
l: A grand name can long outlive the reality it described.
q: Who called the Holy Roman Empire “neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire”?

t: The king who crashed the price of gold
p: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, set out on a pilgrimage to Mecca with a huge caravan.
In Cairo he spent and gave away so much gold that, according to the historian al-Umari, its value stayed low for years. He is often named as one of the richest people in history.
l: Too much money in circulation lowers its value: inflation existed in the 14th century too.
q: What happened in Cairo after Mansa Musa's visit?
The value of gold fell for years
A revolt broke out against him

t: The Library of Alexandria died slowly
p: It did not burn down in one great fire. The blaze of 48 BC, during Caesar's war, damaged it.
Then came scholars expelled by kings, smaller budgets and civil wars. By the time Aurelian devastated the palace quarter in AD 272, it had been in decline for a long time.
l: Institutions of knowledge die of neglect more often than of catastrophe.
q: How did the Library of Alexandria disappear?
Through a slow decline lasting centuries
In a single fire started by Caesar
It was taken apart and moved to Rome

t: The revolution that started with a song
p: On 25 April 1974, just after midnight, a Lisbon radio station played “Grândola, Vila Morena” by Zeca Afonso. It was the agreed signal for the rebel officers.
Within hours the Estado Novo dictatorship, in power for over forty years, collapsed. Crowds put carnations into the barrels of the soldiers' rifles: the Carnation Revolution was born.
l: A signal can be anything, as long as everyone knows what it means.
q: What was the signal for the Carnation Revolution?
A song played on the radio
A cannon shot from the harbour
A speech by the president on TV

t: The Wall fell because of a wrong answer
p: On 9 November 1989 the East German spokesman Günter Schabowski read out a new rule on foreign travel, live on TV. He had not been briefed on the details.
Asked when it took effect, he answered: “Immediately, without delay.” Thousands of Berliners rushed to the crossings, and that night the guards, with no orders, opened the gates.
l: History speeds up when a rigid system stops knowing what to do.
q: What did Schabowski say about when the new rule applied?

t: The man who decided it was a false alarm
p: In the Serpukhov-15 bunker, the Soviet satellite system reported the launch of five American missiles. Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov was supposed to alert his superiors.
He reasoned that a real attack would be massive, not five missiles, and reported it as a fault. He was right: the satellites had mistaken sunlight reflecting off clouds for rockets.
l: An automatic system is only as reliable as the judgement of whoever decides whether to believe it.
q: Why did Petrov think it was a false alarm?
A real attack would have used many more missiles
The ground radars were switched off

t: The “no” that stopped a nuclear torpedo
p: On 27 October 1962 the Soviet submarine B-59, hunted by American ships dropping signalling depth charges, had lost contact with Moscow. The captain wanted to fire a nuclear torpedo.
Firing needed the agreement of the three most senior officers on board. Vasili Arkhipov said no, and the submarine surfaced.
l: Rules that require more than one signature exist for the moments when one person alone would get it wrong.
q: What was needed to fire the nuclear torpedo from B-59?
A vote of the whole crew

t: An eye for an eye, but not for everyone
p: The Code of Hammurabi, carved on a basalt stele now in the Louvre, collects 282 laws. Many follow the principle of retaliation.
If a free man blinds another free man, he loses an eye. But if the victim is someone's slave, paying half the slave's value is enough. Justice depended on social class.
l: Retaliation set a limit on revenge, but it worked differently for each class.
q: In the Code of Hammurabi, the penalty for blinding someone depended on…
The age of the guilty person

t: Magna Carta lasted ten weeks
p: King John granted it under pressure from rebel barons, and after about ten weeks Pope Innocent III declared it void.
It was reissued and revised several times, until it became the symbol of an idea: even the king is subject to the law. Three of its clauses are still in force in English law.
l: A failed document can become a powerful symbol if it expresses a principle.
q: Who annulled Magna Carta a few weeks later?

t: When the Revolution made time decimal
p: After the metric system, the French revolutionaries tried to make time decimal too: days of 10 hours, hours of 100 minutes, minutes of 100 seconds.
Ten-hour clocks were built, but nobody wanted to throw away the old ones and change their habits. The rule was suspended in 1795; the metre, on the other hand, conquered the world.
l: A reform succeeds when its benefits outweigh the cost of changing habits.
q: How many hours were in a day of revolutionary decimal time?

t: A friar put modern accounting in a book
p: In 1494 the Franciscan friar Luca Pacioli, a mathematician and friend of Leonardo, published his “Summa de arithmetica” in Venice.

One chapter described double-entry bookkeeping “the Venetian way”, already used by Italian merchants: every transaction is recorded twice, as debit and credit, so mistakes stand out. Businesses everywhere still use it.
l: Recording everything twice looks redundant: that is exactly what makes errors visible.
q: Who described double-entry bookkeeping in a book printed in 1494?

t: Galileo probably never said “And yet it moves”
p: In 1633 Galileo, condemned by the Holy Office, knelt and renounced the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun.

The famous line of defiance appears in no record of the trial: it first shows up in a book in 1757, over a century later, in a collection by Giuseppe Baretti. Galileo spent his last years under house arrest at Arcetri.
l: The most perfect famous quotes are often added later by the storytellers.
q: When does “And yet it moves” first appear in a book?
In Galileo's letters to his daughter

t: Marco Polo's book was dictated in prison
p: Marco Polo returned to Venice in 1295 after 24 years in Asia. Captured by the Genoese in a war, he met Rustichello da Pisa, a writer of chivalric romances, in jail.
Polo talked and Rustichello wrote, in Franco-Italian: that is how one of the most read books of the Middle Ages was born. Christopher Columbus owned a copy full of notes.
l: Without a cellmate who could write, we might never have heard of Marco Polo's journey.
q: Who did Marco Polo dictate his story to?

t: The crusade that sacked a Christian city
p: The Fourth Crusade was meant to reach the Holy Land, but the crusaders could not pay Venice for the ships.
To settle the debt, Doge Enrico Dandolo, over ninety and almost blind, diverted them first to Zara and then to Constantinople, sacked in 1204. The bronze horses of St Mark's Basilica come from there.
l: A debt can change the course of a holy war: interests and ideals are often tangled together.
q: Where did the Fourth Crusade end up in 1204?

t: Spartacus started with seventy men
p: He escaped from a gladiator school in Capua with about seventy companions armed with kitchen knives. They took refuge on Vesuvius and beat the first troops Rome sent.
In two years the slave army grew to tens of thousands of people. After the defeat, six thousand prisoners were crucified along the Appian Way.
l: A revolt of a few becomes a war when it meets enormous discontent.
q: Where did Spartacus and his men take refuge at the start of the revolt?

t: The first recorded strike
p: Under Ramesses III, the craftsmen of Deir el-Medina, who dug and decorated the royal tombs, went weeks without their grain rations.
They downed tools and sat in front of the temples until the officials paid up. The papyrus that tells the story is kept at the Egyptian Museum in Turin.
l: Strikes are as old as organised work: even the builders of the pharaohs' tombs went on strike.
q: Where is the papyrus of the first recorded strike kept?
At the Egyptian Museum in Turin

t: The pyramids were not built by slaves
p: Next to the pyramids of Giza, archaeologists found the workers' village and their tombs, buried with honour near the pharaoh.
The diary of an inspector named Merer, found at Wadi al-Jarf, describes organised crews moving limestone blocks along canals from the Nile. They were workers fed with bread and beer, often in shifts.
l: Slaves under the whip come from the movies; the sources describe a huge organisation of labour.
q: According to archaeological evidence, who built the pyramids of Giza?

t: The secret weapon nobody can make anymore
p: Around 672 an architect named Kallinikos brought Constantinople an incendiary mixture that burned even on water.
Sprayed from siphons mounted on ships, it destroyed the Arab fleets besieging the city. The recipe was a state secret kept so well that it was lost: its ingredients are still debated today.
l: A secret guarded too well can die with the people who know it.
q: What made Greek fire so feared?

t: The fastest post in the Middle Ages was Mongol
p: The largest contiguous empire in history was held together by the “yam”: a network of stations with fresh horses, food and lodging, a few dozen kilometres apart.
By changing horses, an urgent courier could cover hundreds of kilometres a day. Marco Polo was deeply impressed.
l: An empire is ruled through information: whoever controls communications controls space.

t: The shortest war in history
p: On 27 August 1896 Britain gave an ultimatum to the new Sultan of Zanzibar, who had taken the throne without its consent.
When time ran out, British ships opened fire on the palace. After about forty minutes the sultan had fled and his flag had been lowered. It is remembered as the shortest war ever recorded.
l: When the balance of power is total, a war can last less than lunch.
q: How long did the Anglo-Zanzibar War last?

t: Garibaldi entered Naples by train
p: On 7 September 1860, with the Bourbon army still under arms, Garibaldi reached Naples by train with a few companions, ahead of his troops, and was welcomed by a cheering crowd.
The irony: the kingdom's railways had been built by the Bourbons, who in 1839 had opened Italy's first line, Naples–Portici.
l: Infrastructure built by a regime can serve the people who overthrow it.

t: The Poles broke Enigma first
p: Years before Turing and Bletchley Park, the Polish mathematician Marian Rejewski worked out how Enigma worked using permutation theory.

With Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski he read German messages for years. In July 1939, just before the invasion, the Poles handed their methods and two replica machines to the French and the British.
l: Great achievements often have a forgotten first chapter.
q: Who first broke the Enigma machine?
An officer of the French secret service

t: The rubber army that fooled Hitler
p: For the Normandy landings the Allies invented an army that did not exist, stationed in England opposite Calais: inflatable tanks, fake radio traffic and General Patton in command.
The Spanish double agent Juan Pujol, codename Garbo, confirmed it all to the Germans, who kept troops at Calais for weeks, even after the landings.
l: In war, making the enemy believe what it expects is worth as much as a real army.
q: What was Patton's army opposite Calais?
A fake army created to deceive

t: Twenty-three stab wounds, only one fatal
p: According to Suetonius, the doctor Antistius examined Caesar's body and concluded that of the 23 wounds only one, the second in the chest, had been fatal.
Suetonius writes that Caesar died without a word, though some claimed he said in Greek: “You too, child?” The famous “Et tu, Brute?” is not in the ancient sources.
l: Even the most famous last words in history can be a later addition.
q: According to Antistius, how many of Caesar's 23 wounds were fatal?

t: When Florence banned Arabic numerals
p: Fibonacci had introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe with his “Liber abaci” of 1202.

But in 1299 the Florentine bankers' guild banned them from account books: a 0 could easily be turned into a 6 or a 9, while numbers written out in words were harder to forge. The new digits caught on slowly.
l: Every new technology brings new risks: at first even zero looked like an invitation to fraud.
q: Why did Florence ban Arabic numerals from account books in 1299?

t: The first human object in space was a weapon
p: On 20 June 1944 a V-2 rocket launched vertically from Peenemünde climbed above 170 km: the first human-made object to reach space.
The V-2 killed thousands of people, but even more died among the prisoners forced to build it. After the war its designer, Wernher von Braun, led the development of the Saturn V.
l: The space race was born from a weapon: the same technology can serve destruction or discovery.
q: What was the first human object to reach space?

t: The wisest man, because he knew he knew nothing
p: The oracle of Delphi said no one was wiser than Socrates. Puzzled, he questioned politicians, poets and craftsmen: all of them thought they knew things they did not.
He concluded that his only advantage was not fooling himself. Plato tells the story in the “Apology”; the slogan “I know that I know nothing” is a later summary.
l: Recognising the limits of what you know is the first step to really learning.
q: Why did Socrates think he was wise?
He knew that he did not know
He had studied with the oracle

t: Plato's cave in thirty seconds
p: Some prisoners, chained since birth, see only shadows cast on a wall and take them for reality. One breaks free, goes outside, is blinded by the light and then sees the real world and the sun.
When he goes back to tell the others, they laugh at him and would be ready to kill him. For Plato, this is the image of education.
l: Leaving your certainties behind hurts, and those who do it are often not believed.
q: What does leaving the cave stand for, according to Plato?

t: The Ship of Theseus
p: The Athenians preserved Theseus' ship by replacing its rotten planks one at a time, Plutarch says. When no plank is original any more, is it still the same ship?
Thomas Hobbes added a twist: if someone collected the old planks and rebuilt the ship, which of the two would be Theseus' ship?
l: The identity of a thing, or a person, is not the same as the parts it is made of.
q: Who added the ship rebuilt from the old planks to the puzzle?

t: You can't step into the same river twice
p: For Heraclitus everything flows: the river stays “the same river” precisely because its water keeps changing.

The order of the world comes from change and from the tension between opposites, as in a drawn bow. People called him “the Obscure” for his riddling style; only fragments quoted by other authors survive.
l: What looks stable is often a process that keeps renewing itself.
q: Because he lived in a cave

t: Will Achilles never catch the tortoise?
p: Zeno of Elea, today's Velia in the Cilento, argued that Achilles can never overtake a tortoise with a head start: when he reaches where it was, it has already moved a little further, and so on forever.
Mathematics later showed that infinitely many ever-smaller intervals can add up to a finite time.
l: An argument can look flawless and still lead to absurdity: then look for the hidden mistake.
q: What solves the paradox of Achilles and the tortoise?
Infinitely many terms can have a finite sum

t: Parmenides: change is an illusion
p: Zeno's teacher, Parmenides, wrote a poem in which a goddess reveals the truth to him: what is, is, and what is not, is not.
If nothing can come from nothing or end in nothing, then birth, death and movement are tricks of the senses. Almost every later Greek philosopher starts from this radical challenge.
l: An extreme thesis can be most useful for forcing others to think better.
q: According to Parmenides, what is change?

t: Medicine for the soul in four doses
p: The Epicureans summed up Epicurus' teaching in four remedies: don't fear the gods; don't fear death; what is good is easy to get; pain is bearable.
On death Epicurus wrote: where we are, death is not; where death is, we are not. His “pleasure” meant above all freedom from anxiety.
l: For Epicurus, happiness is not excess but the absence of pain in the body and fear in the mind.

t: The burnt library we are learning to read
p: In the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum, Vesuvius carbonised hundreds of scrolls, many by the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus. Unrolling them destroys them.
Since 2023, using CT scans and artificial intelligence, researchers in the Vesuvius Challenge have been reading words inside scrolls that were never opened. The first word deciphered means “purple”.
l: A new technology can reopen archives we thought were lost forever.
q: What was the first word read inside a closed Herculaneum scroll?

t: What is up to you, and what isn't
p: Epictetus, born a slave and later a teacher of philosophy, opens his “Handbook” like this: some things are up to us, like judgements, desires and choices; others are not, like our body, reputation and public office.
We suffer when we treat the second kind as if it were the first. It is the practical heart of Stoicism.
l: Put your energy into what you can control; accept the rest.
q: According to Epictetus, what is up to us?

t: The diary of an emperor who didn't want readers
p: Marcus Aurelius wrote down his thoughts in Greek during military campaigns along the Danube.
The original title is “To Himself”: exercises to remind himself to be fair, patient and aware of death, not a book for the public. Today they are among the most read philosophy texts in the world.
l: Writing for yourself is a way to train your character, not to show it off.
q: In what language did Marcus Aurelius write his Meditations?

t: Life isn't short: we waste it
p: In “On the Shortness of Life” Seneca notes that we complain life is short, yet we hand out pieces of it to anyone: to pointless commitments, to ambition, to waiting for tomorrow.
No one would let others take their money, yet we let them take our time. To really live, for him, is to spend time with care.
l: Time is the only thing no one can give back to you: guard it like money.
q: What is the thesis of “On the Shortness of Life”?
Life is long if you use it well
Life is too short for philosophy

t: “Stand out of my sunlight”
p: Diogenes of Sinope lived in a large jar, owned almost nothing and walked around in daylight with a lamp, “looking for a man”.
The story goes that Alexander the Great met him and asked what he could do for him. The answer: “Stand out of my sunlight.” For the Cynics, freedom meant needing very little.
l: Someone who needs nothing cannot be bought by anyone.
q: What did Diogenes ask Alexander the Great?
To move out of his sunlight

t: Virtue lies in the middle, but not halfway
p: For Aristotle every virtue is a balance between two vices: courage lies between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between meanness and waste.
But the “golden mean” is not an arithmetic compromise: it depends on the person and the situation. And it is learned by practice, just as you become a lyre player by playing the lyre.
l: Virtues are habits: you become brave by doing brave things.

t: Occam's razor wasn't written by Occam
p: William of Ockham, an English Franciscan friar, kept repeating that we should not assume more entities than necessary.

The famous Latin phrase, “entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem”, only appears in the 1600s, in a commentator. The principle still helps: between two equally good explanations, start with the one with fewer assumptions.
l: The simplest explanation is not always true, but it is the best place to start.

t: I think, therefore I am
p: Descartes decided to doubt everything: his senses, which sometimes deceive, and even mathematics, imagining an evil demon tricking him.
But while he doubts, he thinks, and to think he must exist. The phrase first appears in French, “je pense, donc je suis”, in the “Discourse on Method”; the Latin version came later.
l: Even the most radical doubt has one fixed point: someone is doing the doubting.
q: In what language did the “cogito” first appear?

t: Pascal's wager
p: Blaise Pascal, a pioneer of probability theory, proposed an argument: if you believe in God and God exists, you gain an infinite good; if He does not, you lose little.
If you don't believe and God exists, you lose everything. So it pays to believe. Critics object: which God? And is faith chosen for convenience still faith?
l: When the stakes are infinite the calculation changes, but not everything comes down to calculation.
q: What is Pascal's wager based on?
A logical proof that God exists

t: Who guarantees the sun will rise tomorrow?
p: David Hume noticed that all our predictions rest on experience: the sun has always risen, so it will rise again.
But no logical argument guarantees that the future will resemble the past: we believe it out of habit. This is the “problem of induction”, still open in the philosophy of science.
l: Our certainties about the future are well-founded habits, not proofs.
q: For Hume, why do we believe the future will resemble the past?

t: You can't get an “ought” from an “is”
p: Hume noticed that many authors, after describing how things are, slip without warning into saying how they ought to be.
But a fact on its own does not imply a duty: knowing that people tend to be selfish says nothing about whether it is right to be. This is known as “Hume's law”.
l: Before accepting a moral conclusion, look for the hidden value among the premises.
q: Facts alone do not give you duties

t: The categorical imperative
p: For Kant an action is moral if the rule you follow could hold for everyone: before lying, ask whether you would want a world where everyone lies when it suits them.
Another version says: always treat every person also as an end, never merely as a means. What counts is not the result but the rule.
l: A choice is right if you could will it as a law for everyone.
q: According to Kant, how should every person be treated?
Always also as an end, never merely as a means
By how useful they can be
As a means to the common good

t: Dare to use your own mind
p: In 1784 a Berlin magazine asked: what is Enlightenment? Kant answered that it is humanity's way out of a self-imposed immaturity.
Immaturity means not using your own understanding without someone else's guidance, out of laziness or fear. The motto, taken from Horace: “sapere aude”, dare to know.
l: Thinking for yourself takes less genius than people think, and more courage.

t: Machiavelli never wrote “the end justifies the means”
p: The phrase does not appear in “The Prince”. Machiavelli, in exile, made a ruthless analysis of power: a prince must be both fox and lion, cunning and strong.
And if he cannot be both loved and feared, it is safer to be feared. His novelty was describing politics as it is, not as it should be.
l: Understanding how power really works also helps those who want to limit it.
q: What does Machiavelli say about love and fear?
If you can't have both, it is safer to be feared
A prince should only make himself loved

t: Why do we accept a state?
p: Thomas Hobbes imagined human beings without laws or government, in the “state of nature”: everyone against everyone, no security, a life “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short”.
To escape it, individuals hand part of their freedom to a sovereign who guarantees peace: the Leviathan. He was writing during the English Civil War.
l: We give up a little freedom in exchange for security: it is the deal behind the modern state.
q: How does Hobbes describe life in the state of nature?
Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short

t: The mind is born a blank slate
p: For John Locke we have no innate ideas: at birth the mind is a “tabula rasa”, a blank slate that experience fills in.

In politics he argued that everyone has natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that a government that violates them can rightfully be overthrown. His ideas inspired the American Revolution.
l: If ideas come from experience, education and environment become decisive.
q: What does Locke mean by “tabula rasa”?
The mind at birth, with no innate ideas

t: “Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains”
p: That is how Rousseau's “Social Contract” begins. For him society, with property and inequality, had corrupted human beings.
A government is legitimate only if it expresses the “general will”, the common good the citizens want, not the sum of private interests. His ideas accompanied the French Revolution.
l: A law is legitimate if citizens can recognise it as their own.
q: For Rousseau, when is a government legitimate?
When it expresses the general will
When the king rules by divine right

t: The philosopher banished at 23
p: Baruch Spinoza was expelled from Amsterdam's Jewish community with an extremely harsh ban for his ideas. He lived modestly by grinding lenses for microscopes and telescopes.
In his “Ethics” he identified God with nature, “Deus sive natura”: a necessary, impersonal order. He died at 44, perhaps partly from the glass dust he had breathed.
l: For Spinoza, understanding the causes of what happens to us is the road to freedom.
q: What did Spinoza do for a living?

t: The best of all possible worlds?
p: Leibniz argued that God, being perfect, had chosen the best of all possible worlds, evil included. In 1755 an earthquake destroyed Lisbon and killed tens of thousands of people.
Voltaire replied with “Candide”, in which Dr Pangloss keeps saying that all is for the best while the world collapses around him.
l: An optimism that justifies everything stops explaining anything.
q: Which event pushed Voltaire to mock Leibniz's optimism?

t: “God is dead” was not a victory cry
p: In aphorism 125 of “The Gay Science”, a madman runs into the marketplace with a lantern lit in broad daylight and announces the death of God, while the crowd laughs.
The tone is tragic: “Who will wipe this blood off us?” Nietzsche was describing the collapse of the foundation of European values, and the question it left: what will we replace it with?
l: When a foundation collapses, the task is not to celebrate but to work out what to build.
q: Who announces the death of God in “The Gay Science”?

t: Would you live your life again, forever?
p: Nietzsche proposes an experiment: a demon tells you that you will have to live your life again exactly as it was, every joy and every pain, for all eternity. Would you despair or bless it?
More than a theory about the cosmos, eternal recurrence is a test: live in such a way that you could want every moment to return.
l: A life well lived is one you would want to repeat exactly.
q: What is the point of the eternal recurrence experiment?
To ask whether we would want to live the same life again
To learn to forget the past

t: Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom
p: At the edge of a cliff we don't only fear falling: what unsettles us is knowing we could jump.

For Søren Kierkegaard, anxiety is born this way, from knowing we can choose among endless possibilities, with no guarantees. It is not a flaw to remove: it is the sign that we are free and responsible for who we become.
l: Feeling the weight of choices is the price, and the proof, of freedom.
q: For Kierkegaard, where does anxiety come from?
From knowing we are free to choose
From fear of what others think

t: The porcupine dilemma
p: On a winter's day some porcupines huddle together to keep warm, but they prick each other with their quills and move apart.
The cold draws them back, the spines push them away, until they find a moderate distance. Schopenhauer makes it an image of human relationships: we need others, but too much closeness hurts.
l: In relationships the right distance isn't given: it has to be found.
q: Needing others and the pain of closeness

t: The owl of Minerva flies at dusk
p: The owl was the symbol of Minerva, goddess of wisdom. For Hegel, philosophy is like her: it only takes flight at dusk.
It manages to understand an age when that age is complete and coming to an end. It cannot predict the future or tell the world how it should be: it always arrives a little late.
l: A period of history is only really understood when seen from afterwards.
q: According to Hegel, when does the owl of Minerva take flight?

t: Interpret the world, or change it?
p: In 1845 the young Karl Marx jotted down eleven short critical theses on the philosopher Feuerbach.

The last one says: philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point is to change it. The theses stayed unpublished until 1888, when Engels printed them. That sentence is carved on Marx's grave in London.
l: For Marx, philosophy should not only understand reality but take on the task of changing it.
q: What does the eleventh thesis on Feuerbach say?
The point is to change the world, not just interpret it
Religion is the opium of the people

t: Condemned to be free
p: In a 1945 lecture Sartre summed up existentialism: existence comes before essence. A paper knife is designed before it exists.
A human being instead exists first, then defines themselves through their choices. We have no nature to excuse us: we are “condemned to be free”, and responsible for what we do.
l: You are not what you were born to be: you are what you choose to do.
q: What does Sartre mean by “existence comes before essence”?
We exist first, then define ourselves through choices
God decides in advance who we are

t: One must imagine Sisyphus happy
p: The gods condemned Sisyphus to push a boulder to the top of a mountain, from which it always rolls back down. For Camus this is the image of the human condition: we look for meaning in a universe that does not answer.
The answer is not despair but a clear-eyed revolt: to live fully, knowing. And he concludes: “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”
l: Meaning is not given in advance: it is created by the way we face the struggle.
q: How does Camus end “The Myth of Sisyphus”?
Sisyphus must rebel against the gods

t: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman”
p: With this sentence Simone de Beauvoir separated biology from the role society builds on top of it.

In “The Second Sex” she analysed how woman had been thought of as “the Other” in relation to man, taken as the measure of everything. Placed on the Vatican's Index of banned books, it became a classic of 20th-century thought.
l: Much of what seems natural is built by social habits and expectations.
q: How does de Beauvoir describe the condition of women in “The Second Sex”?
Thought of as “the Other” in relation to man
The same in every age and culture

t: The banality of evil
p: Hannah Arendt followed the trial of Adolf Eichmann, one of the organisers of the Nazi deportations. She expected a monster and found a bureaucrat obsessed with career and procedures.
He seemed unable to think from anyone else's point of view. She concluded that enormous evils can be committed by ordinary people who stop thinking about what they are doing.
l: The worst evil does not need exceptional wickedness: it is enough to stop thinking.
q: What struck Hannah Arendt about Eichmann?
How ordinary he was, like a bureaucrat

t: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent
p: It is the last sentence of Ludwig Wittgenstein's “Tractatus”, finished during the First World War and carried with him into a prison camp at Cassino.
Language, he argued, can describe facts; ethics and the meaning of life lie beyond its limits. Years later he changed his mind: the meaning of a word is its use.
l: Understanding the limits of language helps us see what we can really say.
q: For the later Wittgenstein, what is the meaning of a word?
What it stands for in the world

t: The veil of ignorance
p: Imagine writing the rules of a society without knowing who you will be: rich or poor, healthy or ill, with what talent or background.
John Rawls argued that behind this “veil of ignorance” we would choose fair rules: equal liberties for all, and inequalities only if they improve the lot of the worst off.
l: To know whether a rule is fair, ask yourself if you would accept it without knowing your place.
q: What don't we know behind the “veil of ignorance”?

t: The trolley problem
p: A runaway trolley is about to run over five people. You can switch it onto a track where it will kill one. Would you do it? Almost everyone says yes.
But if stopping it meant pushing a heavy man off a bridge, almost everyone says no, even though the numbers are identical. The dilemma shows we don't judge by numbers alone.
l: For our morality, how harm is caused matters too, not just how much harm.
q: What does the trolley problem show?
We don't judge actions only by their consequences

t: Would you plug into the happiness machine?
p: Robert Nozick imagined a machine that could give you pleasant experiences indistinguishable from reality, for your whole life. Would you plug in? Many people say no.
If so, we don't only want to feel good: we want to actually do things, to be a certain kind of person, to stay in touch with reality.
l: If you refuse the machine, pleasure is not everything for you.
q: What does refusing the experience machine suggest?
We don't only want to feel pleasure

t: The Chinese room: can a machine understand?
p: John Searle imagines himself shut in a room with a rulebook for combining Chinese symbols, a language he doesn't know. Questions in Chinese are passed in; following the rules, he hands back perfect answers.
People outside think he understands Chinese, but he understands nothing. For Searle, manipulating symbols is not enough to understand.
l: Acting as if you understand and really understanding may be two different things.
q: What is the Chinese room meant to show?
Manipulating symbols is not the same as understanding

t: What is time?
p: “If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I don't know.” That is how Saint Augustine opens his inquiry.
The past no longer exists, the future does not exist yet, the present does not last. He concludes that time lives in the soul: memory of the past, attention to the present, expectation of the future.
l: The most familiar things are often the hardest to define.
q: According to Augustine, where is time?
In the soul: memory, attention, expectation
In the regular motion of the stars
Only in the mind of God

t: Thomas Aquinas was kidnapped by his family
p: In Naples, where he was studying, young Thomas decided to join the Dominicans, an order of begging friars.

His noble family wanted him to become an abbot at Montecassino: his brothers seized him and kept him locked up for about a year. He did not give in, and became the most influential theologian of the Middle Ages.
l: Choices that change a life are sometimes paid for with opposition from those closest to us.
q: Why did Thomas Aquinas' family lock him up?
They opposed his joining the Dominicans
He had committed a crime in Naples
He wanted to marry against their will

t: Giordano Bruno's infinite universe
p: The friar from Nola, Giordano Bruno, held that the universe was infinite and full of countless worlds, with stars like our sun.
Tried for heresy, over theological claims as well as cosmological ones, he refused to recant. On 17 February 1600 he was burned alive in Campo de' Fiori, where his statue stands today.
l: Some insights arrive centuries before the tools to test them.
q: What did Giordano Bruno claim about the universe?
It was infinite, with countless worlds
The Earth was its motionless centre

t: We only truly know what we make
p: The Neapolitan philosopher Giambattista Vico formulated the principle “verum ipsum factum”: the true is the same as the made.
That is why we can understand history, made by human beings, better than nature, made by God. In his “New Science” he described history as a cycle of rises and returns, “corsi e ricorsi”.
l: You truly understand something when you know how to build it.
q: The true is the same as what has been made

t: The prison where you never know if you're watched
p: Jeremy Bentham designed the Panopticon: cells arranged in a circle around a tower from which a guard can see everyone without being seen.
Not knowing when they are watched, the prisoners behave as if they always were. In 1975 Michel Foucault made it the symbol of a power that pushes us to watch ourselves.
l: The mere chance of being watched is enough to change behaviour.
q: What principle is the Panopticon based on?

t: Better Socrates dissatisfied
p: John Stuart Mill was a utilitarian: what is right is what produces the most happiness. But for him not all pleasures are equal.

He wrote that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. Those who know both kinds of pleasure, he argued, choose those of the intellect.
l: The quality of pleasures matters, not just the quantity.
q: What did Mill add to utilitarianism?

t: A scientific theory must be able to be proved wrong
p: For Karl Popper no number of white swans proves that all swans are white, but a single black one is enough to disprove it.
A theory is scientific if it says what would make it false. Einstein's relativity took risks, with precise predictions to test; a theory that explains any result, for Popper, says nothing.
l: A theory that can never be wrong isn't saying anything precise.
q: What makes a theory scientific, for Popper?
It can be disproved by an observation
The number of confirmations it has
The authority of whoever proposes it

t: How scientific ideas really change
p: Thomas Kuhn noticed that science doesn't advance only by piling up discoveries. For long periods scientists work inside a shared “paradigm”; when anomalies pile up, a revolution comes, as from Ptolemy to Copernicus.
Kuhn quoted Max Planck: a new scientific truth often wins because its opponents eventually die.
l: Scientific progress has a human side too: habits, communities, generations.
q: What does Kuhn call the shared framework scientists work within?

t: Is it good because the gods want it?
p: Socrates asks Euthyphro: is something holy because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is holy?

If the first, goodness is arbitrary: the gods could want anything. If the second, goodness exists independently of the gods. For 2,400 years the dilemma has haunted every debate on religion and morality.
l: If good depends only on a command, whoever commands can make it arbitrary.
q: What does the Euthyphro dilemma ask?
Whether goodness depends on the gods or comes before them
Who created the world and why

t: Would you be just if you were invisible?
p: The shepherd Gyges finds a ring that makes him invisible and uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king and take the throne.
In the “Republic”, Glaucon challenges Socrates: anyone with that ring would act the same way; we are just only out of fear of the consequences. The rest of the dialogue tries to prove him wrong.
l: Character shows in what you would do if no one could ever find out.
q: What does Glaucon argue with the myth of Gyges?
We are just only out of fear of the consequences
The gods always punish the guilty

t: Winning without fighting
p: “The Art of War”, attributed to Sun Tzu, holds that the best victory is won without a battle: first defeat the enemy's plans, then their alliances, only then their army.
Besieging walled cities is the worst option. Knowing the enemy and knowing yourself counts for more than strength.
l: The best strategy makes the battle unnecessary.
q: According to Sun Tzu, what is the worst option?

t: War as the continuation of politics
p: Carl von Clausewitz, a Prussian officer who had fought against Napoleon, wrote that war is the continuation of politics by other means: a tool serving political goals, not an end in itself.
He also described “friction”: a thousand small hitches that make even the simplest action difficult. “On War” came out after his death.
l: Every plan runs into the friction of reality: whoever expects it makes fewer mistakes.
q: The small hitches that complicate every action
A head-on clash between two armies
The economic exhaustion of a nation

t: The golden rule, five centuries before the Gospels
p: A disciple asked Confucius whether there was one word to live by for a whole life. He answered: “reciprocity”, that is, do not do to others what you would not want done to you.
The same idea appears in many traditions, from Greece to India. For Confucius, social order grows out of respectful relationships, starting with the family.
l: Putting yourself in someone else's shoes is the most widespread moral rule in the world.
q: Which word did Confucius name as a guide for a whole life?

t: A journey of a thousand miles begins with one step
p: The saying comes from the “Tao Te Ching”, attributed to Laozi. In the original the unit is the “li”, about half a kilometre: even the greatest undertakings grow from small actions.
Taoism invites us to follow the natural course of things: water, soft and yielding, wears away rock in the long run.
l: Great results are built from small, steady gestures.
q: What does Taoism teach with the image of water?
What is soft and yielding wins in the long run

t: Hypatia, mathematician and philosopher
p: In Alexandria, Hypatia taught mathematics, astronomy and Neoplatonic philosophy to pagan and Christian students alike, and the city's magistrates consulted her.
In 415, during a political clash between Bishop Cyril and the prefect Orestes, a Christian mob attacked and killed her. She has become a symbol of freedom of thought.
l: Those who bridge different worlds become targets when those worlds clash.
q: What did Hypatia teach in Alexandria?

t: The philosophy that consoles in prison
p: Boethius had been one of King Theodoric's most powerful officials. Accused of treason, while awaiting execution he wrote “The Consolation of Philosophy”.
Philosophy appears to him as a woman and reminds him that Fortune turns like a wheel. Outward goods come and go; what really matters is within us.
l: What luck gives you, luck can take back: true wealth is inside.

t: The man who invented the essay
p: At 38 Michel de Montaigne retired to the tower of his castle, among his books, and began writing about himself: his habits, his fears, his reading.
He called those texts “Essais”, attempts. His motto was a question: “Que sais-je?”, what do I know? He founded a literary genre built on doubt and self-observation.
l: Studying yourself honestly is a way to understand human beings.

t: When does a heap stop being a heap?
p: One grain of sand is not a heap. Adding one grain to something that is not a heap doesn't make it one. Yet, grain after grain, at some point there is a heap.
The sorites paradox, attributed to Eubulides, shows that many words, like “bald”, “tall” or “rich”, have no sharp boundaries.
l: Many concepts have blurry edges: demanding an exact threshold creates paradoxes.
q: What does the sorites paradox show?

t: The donkey that starved between two haystacks
p: A hungry donkey stands exactly halfway between two identical haystacks. With no reason to prefer one, it never chooses, and starves.

The example bears the name of the philosopher Jean Buridan, but it doesn't appear in his writings; Aristotle already spoke of a man between food and drink. It mocks the idea that every choice needs a reason.
l: Sometimes choosing at random is more rational than not choosing.
q: It can't choose between two identical options
The hay in both piles is poisoned

t: Rereading isn't enough: testing yourself is
p: In an experiment, some students reread a text several times; others read it once and then tried to recall it from memory. After five minutes, the rereaders won.
After a week, those who had tested themselves remembered about 61% against 40%. That's why this app sends you a review every now and then.
l: Every time you pull an idea out of memory, you make it stronger.
q: What did Roediger and Karpicke's experiment show?
Testing yourself makes memories last longer than rereading
Rereading is the most effective technique

t: The forgetting curve
p: Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of nonsense syllables, like “WID” or “ZOF”, and measured how many he forgot over time.
The loss was very fast in the first hours and days, then slowed down. He also found that reviews spread out over time work far better than many repetitions crammed together.
l: Review a little and often, at growing intervals: it is the most efficient way not to forget.
q: What did Ebbinghaus discover about memory?
We forget fast right after learning
We forget at a constant rate
Nonsense syllables are easier to remember

t: Those who know little tend to overrate themselves
p: In a 1999 study, the participants who did worst on logic and grammar tests rated themselves above average, while the best slightly underrated themselves.
The idea: to recognise your own incompetence you need exactly the skills you lack. But beware: part of the effect may be a statistical artefact, and the debate is open.
l: Confidence is not proof of competence: the more you know a field, the more you see what you're missing.
q: How did the weakest participants rate themselves?

t: A random number changes your estimates
p: In an experiment, a rigged wheel stopped on either 10 or 65. Then participants were asked what percentage of UN member countries were African.
Those who had seen 10 answered 25% on average; those who had seen 65 answered 45%. An obviously irrelevant number acted as an “anchor”. It happens in negotiations and with prices too.
l: The first number you hear sways your judgement, even when you know it's random.
q: What does the rigged wheel experiment show?

t: Losing hurts more than winning pleases
p: According to Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, losses weigh psychologically about twice as much as equal gains.
That's why many people turn down a coin-toss bet where they could win 150 euros or lose 100, even though on average it pays. It also explains why people hold on to losing investments for too long.
l: We fear losses more than we love gains: noticing it helps us decide better.
q: About how much do losses weigh compared with equal gains?

t: The Concorde fallacy
p: The Concorde, the Anglo-French supersonic airliner, was clearly losing money while still in development, yet the governments kept funding it: they had spent too much to stop.
This is the sunk cost fallacy: letting money, time or effort already spent decide the future. All that counts is what you can still gain or lose.
l: What you've spent won't come back: decide by looking forward, not back.
q: What does the sunk cost fallacy describe?
Carrying on only because you've already invested
Always saving money no matter what

t: When the group is wrong, and you follow it
p: Solomon Asch asked which of three lines was as long as a sample line: a very easy question. But the room was full of accomplices who all gave the wrong answer.
About three participants in four went along with the group at least once. Yet a single accomplice who disagreed was enough to make the conformity collapse.
l: A single voice that breaks ranks makes it easier for everyone to say what they see.
q: What sharply reduced conformity in Asch's experiments?

t: How far will we obey?
p: Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to give ever-stronger electric shocks to a “learner” who made mistakes, actually an actor.

In the best-known version about two in three went all the way to the maximum, 450 volts, just because the experimenter calmly insisted. The study is criticised for its method and ethics, but it remains a warning about authority.
l: An authority that seems legitimate can push ordinary people to do what they never would.
q: How many participants went up to 450 volts in the best-known version?

t: The marshmallow test predicts less than it seems
p: In Walter Mischel's famous experiments, children who could wait to get two treats instead of one seemed to do better as adults.
A 2018 replication, with a larger and more varied sample, found a much weaker link, largely explained by family background and economic conditions.
l: A famous result is not final: replications with bigger samples can cut it down to size.
q: What did the 2018 replication of the marshmallow test find?
A much weaker link with success

t: Why flying scares us more than driving
p: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. A plane crash fills the front pages for days; everyday road accidents don't.
So flying seems more dangerous, even though per kilometre it is far safer than the car. This is the availability heuristic.
l: What you remember most easily is not necessarily what happens most often.
q: What is the availability heuristic based on?

t: When a measure becomes a target
p: Goodhart's law, in its best-known form, says: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
If a hospital is rewarded for short waits in the emergency department, it can find ways to lower the number without treating people better. The same goes for grades, business indicators and rankings.
l: Every number used as a reward is sooner or later gamed.
q: A measure used as a target becomes unreliable

t: The doctor who asked colleagues to wash their hands
p: Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that in a Vienna maternity ward, women died of fever far more often when attended by doctors coming straight from autopsies.
He made them wash their hands in a chlorine solution and deaths plummeted. Many colleagues mocked him. Rejecting evidence that contradicts habits is now called the “Semmelweis reflex”.
l: Inconvenient evidence is not enough to change habits: you also have to convince the people who must change.
q: What did Semmelweis make the doctors do?
Wash their hands in a chlorine solution

t: Learn a new word and you'll see it everywhere
p: You discover a name or buy a car, and suddenly you come across it everywhere. There aren't more of them: your attention has changed and now notices them, and memory records every new confirmation.
The linguist Arnold Zwicky called it the “frequency illusion”; online it is also known as the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon.
l: What you notice depends on what you are looking for, not only on what is there.
q: Why does a word you've just learned seem to appear everywhere?
Your attention changes, not the frequency

t: The number 150
p: The anthropologist Robin Dunbar noticed a link between the size of the neocortex in primates and the size of their groups.
For humans he estimated about 150 stable relationships that one person can really keep up. It is a much-debated hypothesis: later studies found wide margins of uncertainty.
l: Social abilities have limits: even the biggest networks rest on a small core.
q: How many stable relationships does Dunbar's number estimate?

t: Measuring the Earth with a shadow
p: Eratosthenes knew that in Syene, at noon on the summer solstice, the sun lit up the bottom of wells. That same day in Alexandria, a stick cast a shadow of about 7 degrees: one fiftieth of a circle.
He multiplied the distance between the two cities by 50 and got the Earth's circumference, probably with only a small error.
l: With the right idea and simple measurements you can work out something enormous.
q: What angle did the shadow make in Alexandria?

t: The 1202 alarm during the Moon landing
p: Minutes before touching down on the Moon, the lunar module's computer began flashing alarms 1202 and 1201: it was overloaded.
The software, written at MIT by the team led by Margaret Hamilton, was designed to drop less important tasks and keep the vital ones. Houston gave the go-ahead: they could carry on.
l: A robust system isn't one that never fails, but one that knows what to sacrifice.
q: What did the Apollo 11 software do when it was overloaded?
It dropped the less important tasks
It handed control to Houston's computer

t: The “beep” that frightened America
p: Sputnik 1 was a 58-centimetre, 84-kilogram sphere with four antennas. It only sent out an intermittent radio signal that amateur radio operators all over the world could pick up.
That was enough: the United States realised that a rocket able to put a satellite in orbit could hit any point on the planet. NASA was founded the following year.
l: A technological demonstration can weigh as much as a weapon, for what it suggests.
q: Which US agency was founded the year after Sputnik?

t: The first flight was shorter than a Boeing 747
p: On 17 December 1903 the Wright brothers' Flyer flew for 12 seconds and about 37 metres: less than the wingspan of a Boeing 747. The same day, on the fourth attempt, they reached 59 seconds and 260 metres.
Their real stroke of genius was control: warping the wings to bank the plane and keep it balanced.
l: Flying wasn't just an engine problem: the breakthrough was learning to control the flight.
q: How long did the Wright brothers' first flight last?

t: Italy reached orbit before almost everyone
p: The San Marco 1 satellite, designed by Luigi Broglio's team, was launched on an American Scout rocket by an all-Italian crew.

Italy thus became the third country, after the USSR and the United States, to put a satellite into orbit with its own launch team. Then came the San Marco platform, a launch base at sea off the coast of Kenya.
l: With the right alliances, even a mid-sized country can join a superpower race early.
q: Who led the San Marco project?

t: “Get the girl to check the numbers”
p: Before his orbital flight, astronaut John Glenn asked for the trajectories worked out by the new electronic computers to be checked by hand by Katherine Johnson, an African American NASA mathematician: “If she says they're good, I'm ready to go.”
Back then “computer” was also a job: people, often women, who did the calculations.
l: Trust in a new system is also built through human checks.
q: What did the word “computer” also mean at NASA back then?

t: The probe lost to a units mix-up
p: The Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in the Martian atmosphere in 1999. Ground software supplied thruster impulses in pound-force seconds, while the navigation system expected newton-seconds.
For months the trajectory drifted slightly, until the probe passed too close to the planet. It had cost about 125 million dollars.
l: Technical disasters are often born at the interfaces between different teams.
q: Why was the Mars Climate Orbiter lost?
A mix-up between imperial and metric units
A failure of the main engine

t: 37 seconds and a number that was too big
p: On its first launch, on 4 June 1996, Ariane 5 self-destructed 37 seconds after lift-off.

Its inertial reference software, reused from Ariane 4, converted a horizontal velocity value from 64 bits into a 16-bit integer: the number was too big and overflowed. The backup system, identical, failed in exactly the same way.
l: Reusing proven code is safe only if the assumptions it was written for still hold.
q: What caused the failure of the first Ariane 5?
An overflow in a number conversion
A wrong command from the ground

t: “Where is everybody?”
p: At lunch with some colleagues, Enrico Fermi asked a simple question: the galaxy has billions of stars and billions of years. If even one civilisation had learned to travel between stars, it would have had time to reach us.
So why don't we see anyone? The Fermi paradox still has no answer.
l: Sometimes the absence of evidence is itself a fact that needs explaining.
q: What does the Fermi paradox ask?
Why we don't see alien civilisations
How many stars the galaxy has

t: The myth of the bumblebee that shouldn't fly
p: In 1934 the entomologist Antoine Magnan cited a calculation according to which bumblebee flight was impossible.

The calculation treated the wings like the rigid wings of a plane, while insects flap them very fast, creating vortices that give extra lift. The physics wasn't wrong: the model applied to the problem was.
l: If reality contradicts the calculation, it's the model that is wrong.
q: Why was the calculation about bumblebee flight wrong?
It treated the wings like a plane's rigid wings
Bumblebees are too heavy to fly

t: The first photo of a shock wave
p: The physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach, with Peter Salcher, was the first to photograph the shock waves of a bullet faster than sound, using extremely brief spark flashes.
That's why the ratio between an object's speed and the speed of sound is called the Mach number. His philosophical ideas also influenced the young Einstein.
l: Physics and philosophy can live in the same head, and feed each other.
q: What does the Mach number measure?
An object's speed compared with the speed of sound

t: The mould that came back from holiday
p: Back from holiday, Alexander Fleming found a dish of bacteria contaminated by a mould, with an empty ring all around it: the mould was killing them.
But for years penicillin remained a lab curiosity. Only in the 1940s did Howard Florey and Ernst Chain manage to produce it and use it as a drug, saving millions of lives.
l: A chance discovery becomes a revolution only if someone makes it usable.
q: Who turned penicillin into a usable drug?

t: You can't see the Great Wall from space
p: It is very long, but usually only a few metres wide and the same colour as the ground: from low orbit, about 400 kilometres up, it blends into the landscape.
In 2003 China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said he had not been able to see it. Motorways, airports and cities lit up at night, on the other hand, stand out clearly.
l: Big doesn't mean visible: contrast matters, not just length.
q: Why is the Great Wall hard to see from orbit?
It is narrow and the same colour as the ground
It is covered by clouds all year

t: Schrödinger's cat was a criticism
p: Schrödinger imagined a cat shut in a box with a device that kills it if an atom decays. On one reading of quantum mechanics, until someone looks, the atom is in a superposition of states.
So the cat would be alive and dead at the same time. Schrödinger wanted to show how absurd it was to extend that idea to everyday objects.
l: A thought experiment invented to mock an idea can become its symbol.
q: Why did Schrödinger come up with the cat experiment?
To criticise an interpretation of quantum mechanics
To prove that cats are quantum

t: Gagarin didn't land inside his capsule
p: The Vostok 1 flight lasted 108 minutes, one orbit around the Earth. During the descent, at about 7 kilometres up, Yuri Gagarin was ejected from the capsule and landed by parachute.
For years the Soviets kept it quiet: under the rules of the time, an aviation record only counted if the pilot landed aboard his craft.
l: Even the most famous records hide details kept quiet for the sake of the rules.
q: How did Yuri Gagarin land in 1961?
On a runway, like a plane

t: The Mona Lisa became famous when it vanished
p: On 21 August 1911 the Mona Lisa disappeared from the Louvre. It had been taken by Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian decorator who had worked there.

He hid it in a trunk for two years, and in 1913 tried to sell it to a Florence antiques dealer, who called the police. With newspapers around the world following the story, the theft made it the most famous painting on the planet.
l: A work's fame also depends on the stories that happen around it.
q: Who stole the Mona Lisa in 1911?

t: Michelangelo's David came from a rejected block
p: The marble for the David had been quarried decades earlier and roughed out by other sculptors, including Agostino di Duccio, who gave up: it was tall, narrow and weathered. People called it “the Giant”.
In 1501 the 26-year-old Michelangelo took on the challenge, and in three years carved the most famous statue of the Renaissance.
l: Where others see waste, talent sees a possibility.
q: What was Michelangelo's David carved from?
A block roughed out and abandoned by others
Fresh marble he chose at Carrara
Three blocks of marble joined together

t: Michelangelo didn't paint the Sistine Chapel lying down
p: The image of the artist lying on his back on the scaffolding is a myth. Michelangelo painted the ceiling standing up, on a platform he designed himself, with his head bent back for hours.
In a mocking sonnet he described his beard pointing at the sky and his back bent like a bow. It took him four years, from 1508 to 1512.
l: The most romantic images of genius often hide gruelling physical work.
q: In what position did Michelangelo paint the Sistine ceiling?
Standing, with his head bent back

t: Seven works of mercy in one painting
p: On the run from Rome after a killing, Caravaggio arrived in Naples and painted a canvas for the Pio Monte della Misericordia.
It packs all seven corporal works of mercy into a single night-time alley. The painting is still there, on the altar it was painted for, a few steps from the cathedral.
l: Caravaggio brought the sacred into the alleys, with the faces of ordinary people.
q: Where is Caravaggio's “Seven Works of Mercy”?
At the Pio Monte della Misericordia in Naples

t: Pinocchio was meant to end up hanged
p: “The Adventures of Pinocchio” came out in instalments in a children's magazine from 1881. In the first version the story ended at chapter XV: the Cat and the Fox hang the puppet from an oak tree.
Readers protested and Collodi picked the story up again: then came the Land of Toys, the Terrible Dogfish, which is not a whale, and the happy ending.
l: One of the happiest endings in children's literature was born from a readers' protest.
q: How did the first serialised version of Pinocchio end?
With the puppet hanged from an oak
With Pinocchio becoming a real boy
With Geppetto swallowed by the Dogfish

t: Frankenstein was born in the year without a summer
p: In 1815 the eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia cooled the climate across half the world, and the summer of 1816 in Europe was cold and rainy.
Stuck indoors in a villa on Lake Geneva, Lord Byron challenged his guests to a horror-story contest. Eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley began “Frankenstein” there; it was published in 1818.
l: An eruption on the other side of the world can change the climate, and even literature.
q: What made the European summer of 1816 cold and rainy?

t: Dante didn't call it “Divine”
p: Dante simply called his poem “Commedia”: a story that begins badly, in Hell, and ends well, in Paradise, written in the everyday language rather than Latin.
The adjective “divine” was first used by Giovanni Boccaccio, a great admirer of Dante. It only appeared in the title in an edition printed in Venice in 1555.
l: The title everyone knows was a reader's tribute, not the author's choice.
q: Who first used the adjective “divine” for the Comedy?

t: Italy's anthem only became official in 2017
p: Goffredo Mameli wrote “Il Canto degli Italiani” in 1847, at twenty; the music is by Michele Novaro. Mameli died in 1849 fighting for the Roman Republic.
From 1946 the song was used as a “provisional” national anthem: it only became official by law in December 2017.
l: Even symbols that seem eternal went through a long provisional phase.
q: Since when has Mameli's hymn been Italy's anthem by law?

t: The Italian tricolour was born in Reggio Emilia
p: On 7 January 1797 the congress of the Cispadane Republic, meeting in Reggio Emilia, adopted a green, white and red flag.
It was the first time the tricolour became the symbol of an Italian state. The model was the French tricolour. Every 7 January Italy celebrates Flag Day.
l: National symbols are born in precise places and moments, before they belong to everyone.
q: Where was the tricolour first adopted as a state flag?

t: “Ciao” means “I am your slave”
p: The world's most famous Italian greeting comes from the Venetian “s-ciào”, slave: short for “s-ciào vostro”, your servant, a polite formula.
In the 1800s it spread through Lombardy as a friendly greeting, then across Italy and the world. “Servus”, still used in Austria and Bavaria, followed the same path.
l: Many greetings begin as formulas of submission that turn affectionate over time.
q: Which Venetian word does “ciao” come from?

t: “Sincere” doesn't come from “without wax”
p: The story goes that Roman sculptors hid flaws in marble with wax, and that statues “sine cera”, without wax, were the honest ones.
It's a nice story, but it's a folk etymology. “Sincere” comes from the Latin “sincerus”, meaning pure, unmixed. Words attract invented stories just like famous people do.
l: An etymology that is too perfect is often invented.
q: Where does the word “sincere” really come from?

t: The word “robot” comes from a Czech play
p: In 1920 the writer Karel Čapek published “R.U.R.”, a play about artificial workers who rebel against humans.
To name them he used “robot”, from the Czech “robota”, forced labour, a word suggested by his brother Josef. Within a few years it was in every language, long before a real robot existed.
l: Sometimes the word arrives before the technology, and shapes how we imagine it.
q: What does the Czech word “robota” mean?

t: “OK” began as a journalists' joke
p: In the 1830s Boston newspapers played with abbreviations of deliberately misspelled words. “O.K.” stood for “oll korrect”, a joke spelling of “all correct”, and appeared in a newspaper in 1839.
The fad would have faded if, in 1840, President Van Buren, nicknamed “Old Kinderhook”, hadn't used it as a campaign slogan.
l: The most widespread words in the world can be born from a game meant to disappear.
q: “Oll korrect”, a joke spelling of all correct

t: A Florentine merchant used the @ before email
p: In 1971 Ray Tomlinson chose the @ sign to separate user and computer in the first networked email.

But the sign is much older: in a letter of 1536 the Florentine merchant Francesco Lapi used it for the amphora, a unit for measuring wine. Italians call it a snail; in Polish it's a little monkey, in Hebrew a strudel.
l: Symbols we think are modern often have centuries of history behind them.
q: What did the @ stand for in Francesco Lapi's 1536 letter?
An amphora, a unit for measuring wine

t: The first text message said “Merry Christmas”
p: On 3 December 1992 engineer Neil Papworth sent the first SMS in history from a computer to the phone of a Vodafone executive in the UK: “Merry Christmas”.
The recipient couldn't reply, because phones couldn't yet type messages. The 160-character limit came from tests on the typical length of postcards and telex messages.
l: Every mass technology starts with a small, almost homely gesture.
q: What did the first text message say?

t: The first computer “bug” was a real moth
p: On 9 September 1947 the technicians of the Harvard Mark II computer, in Grace Hopper's team, found a moth stuck in a relay.
They taped it into the logbook with the note: “First actual case of bug being found.” The word “bug” for a technical fault had existed since Edison's time: that was the joke.
l: Technical jargon often grows out of in-jokes that then become everyday language.
q: What was found inside the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947?
A moth stuck in a relay
A calculation error in the program

t: Pizza Margherita, between history and legend
p: According to tradition, in June 1889 the pizza maker Raffaele Esposito made Queen Margherita a pizza with tomato, mozzarella and basil, the colours of the flag, and named it after her.
Some historians doubt the story; similar pizzas were certainly sold in Naples before then. Since 2017 the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo has been UNESCO heritage.
l: Many “official” origins are embellished stories: the product was already there.
q: The art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo

t: Italian cooking lived for centuries without tomatoes
p: The tomato arrived from the Americas in the 1500s and for decades was grown mostly as an ornamental plant: many people thought it was unhealthy.
The first printed Italian recipe for tomato sauce dates from 1692: the cook Antonio Latini published it in Naples, calling it “tomato sauce in the Spanish style”.
l: Many traditions that seem eternal are only a few centuries old.
q: When was the first printed Italian recipe for tomato sauce published?

t: Marco Polo didn't bring pasta from China
p: The myth was spread mainly by an American pasta-industry magazine in 1929.

Yet as early as 1154 the Arab geographer al-Idrisi described the production of “itriyya”, dried string-shaped pasta, at Trabia in Sicily, exported all over the Mediterranean: more than a century before Marco Polo's journey.
l: Exotic origins invented by marketing stick in our minds more than documents do.
q: Where did al-Idrisi describe dried pasta production in 1154?

t: The first espresso machine came from Turin
p: In 1884 Angelo Moriondo, who owned cafés in Turin, patented a machine that used steam and pressurised water to make coffee in moments. He built only a few, for his own bars.
Successful bar machines arrived in Milan in the early 1900s, with the patents of Luigi Bezzera and Desiderio Pavoni.
l: A good idea isn't enough: someone has to make it mass-producible.
q: Who patented the first espresso machine in 1884?

t: Why a marathon is 42.195 km
p: At the first modern Olympics, in Athens, the marathon was roughly forty kilometres long.

At the London Games of 1908 the course started at Windsor Castle and finished in front of the royal box in the stadium: 42.195 km, or 26 miles and 385 yards. That distance became the official standard in 1921.
l: Many standards come from a one-off choice that nobody ever changed.
q: Why is a marathon 42.195 km long?
Because of the course of the 1908 London Games
It's the exact distance from Marathon to Athens
A rule from the ancient Games

t: The ancient Olympics lasted more than a thousand years
p: Tradition dates the first Olympics to 776 BC, at Olympia, in honour of Zeus. During the Games a sacred truce guaranteed safe travel for athletes and spectators.
Athletes competed naked and the prize was an olive wreath. The contests went on under Roman rule too, at least until the end of the 4th century AD.
l: The ancient world also knew how to pause its wars, when there was a shared reason.
q: What was the prize for winners at the ancient Olympics?

t: Australia is wider than the Moon
