p: The Moon's diameter is about 3,475 km; Australia measures about 4,000 km from east to west.

The comparison is surprising partly because Australia looks small on the most common maps: the Mercator projection enlarges lands near the poles, like Greenland, and shrinks those closer to the equator.
l: The maps we use every day distort the proportions of the world.
q: Why does Australia look smaller than it is on common maps?
Mercator enlarges lands near the poles
Maps cut off its west coast

t: The world's largest desert is Antarctica
p: For geographers a desert is not a hot, sandy place but a region with very little precipitation.
By that definition the largest desert on Earth is Antarctica, about 14 million square kilometres, followed by the Arctic. The Sahara, the largest hot desert, only comes third.
l: Everyday words and scientific words don't always mean the same thing.
q: What is the largest desert in the world?

t: One lake holds a fifth of the world's fresh water
p: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world: it goes down more than 1,600 metres. It is also one of the oldest, about 25 million years old.
Although its surface area is similar to Belgium's, it holds on its own about a fifth of the liquid fresh water on the Earth's surface.
l: Depth matters more than size: Baikal is as wide as a small country, but deeper than any other lake.
q: How much of the liquid fresh water on Earth's surface does Baikal hold?

t: The peak farthest from Earth's centre isn't Everest
p: Everest, at 8,849 metres, is the highest mountain above sea level. But the Earth is flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator.
So the summit farthest from the planet's centre is Chimborazo, in Ecuador, “only” 6,263 metres high. From its top you are about two kilometres further from the centre than on Everest.
l: The answer to “which is the highest?” depends on how you choose to measure.
q: Which peak is farthest from the centre of the Earth?

t: The world's oldest republic is surrounded by Italy
p: According to tradition, San Marino was founded in 301 by Marinus, a Christian stonemason from Dalmatia who took refuge on Mount Titano.
Its Statutes of 1600 are considered the oldest written constitution still in force. It has two heads of state, the Captains Regent, who serve for only six months.
l: Short terms and power split in two: an old remedy against those who want to rule too long.
q: How long do San Marino's Captains Regent serve?

t: The world's smallest state was born in 1929
p: Vatican City covers about 0.44 square kilometres, less than many city parks.

It has only been an independent state since 1929, when the Lateran Pacts between the Holy See and Italy settled the “Roman Question”, opened by the capture of Rome in 1870. Its Swiss Guard, however, has served since 1506.
l: A tiny territory can carry enormous weight if it stands for something to many people.
q: When did Vatican City become an independent state?

t: On Venus a day lasts longer than a year
p: A year on Venus lasts about 225 days on Earth, but spinning once on its axis takes 243. It also rotates the opposite way to the Earth: there, the Sun rises in the west.
Under clouds of sulphuric acid the temperature tops 460 °C, hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
l: Being close to the Sun isn't enough to explain the heat: the atmosphere matters too.
q: On Venus, where does the Sun rise?

t: Bananas are berries; strawberries aren't
p: In botany, a berry is a fleshy fruit that grows from a single ovary and contains seeds. So bananas, tomatoes, kiwis and even aubergines are berries.
The strawberry, on the other hand, is a “false fruit”: the red part is the swollen receptacle of the flower, and the true fruits are the little yellow dots on the surface.
l: Kitchen categories and scientific categories follow different logics.
q: What are the true fruits of the strawberry?
The little yellow dots on the surface

t: Cathedral glass doesn't flow
p: People say old stained-glass windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows like a liquid.

It doesn't: at room temperature it would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag visibly. The panes were uneven because of how they were made, and glaziers often fitted the thicker edge at the bottom.
l: A true observation can be explained by a false theory.
q: Why are old window panes often thicker at the bottom?
They were uneven and fitted that way
Glass flows slowly over the centuries

t: Bulls don't get angry at red
p: Cattle see colours in a limited way and can't make out red well. In tests, bulls charge red, blue or white cloths just the same: what provokes them is the movement.
The red of the matador's cape is mostly for show, and it also hides bloodstains.
l: We often credit animals with our perceptions instead of theirs.
q: What makes the bull charge in a bullfight?

t: The Amazon isn't the lung that gives us oxygen
p: You often read that the Amazon produces 20% of the planet's oxygen. In fact the forest uses up almost all the oxygen it produces, through the respiration of plants, animals and microbes.
About half of the oxygen produced each year comes from ocean phytoplankton. The Amazon is still vital for other things: climate, rainfall, carbon and biodiversity.
l: A good cause is better defended with real data.
q: Why isn't the Amazon the planet's “lung”?
It uses up almost all the oxygen it produces

t: 1,936.27: the number that ended the lira
p: The euro was born as a currency at the end of the 1990s, but only for markets and banks.

Coins and notes reached people's pockets on 1 January 2002, at a fixed rate of 1,936.27 lire to one euro. For two months both currencies circulated together: the lira stopped being legal tender on 28 February 2002.
l: You can change a currency in a day; mental habits take years.
q: How many lire was one euro worth?

t: The first stamp changed who paid for the post
p: Before 1840 in Britain it was often the recipient who paid for a letter, according to distance. Rowland Hill proposed a single prepaid rate.
On 6 May 1840 the Penny Black came into use: the first adhesive stamp, with Queen Victoria's profile. Within a few years the number of letters sent had multiplied.
l: Making a service simple and cheap can make its use explode.
q: What changed with the Penny Black in 1840?
Postage was paid in advance at a single rate
You could only send post within London

t: Trains unified the world's clocks
p: Until the 1800s every city kept its own time, set by local solar noon: Turin and Venice were almost twenty minutes apart.
With the railways that chaos became unmanageable. In 1884 an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the prime meridian. Italy adopted Central European Time in 1893.
l: The conventions we take for granted were born to solve very concrete problems.
q: Which meridian was chosen as zero in 1884?

t: Beethoven didn't hear the applause for his Ninth
p: At the premiere of the Ninth Symphony, on 7 May 1824 in Vienna, Beethoven was by then almost completely deaf. He stood on stage beside the conductor, following the score.
At the end he was still facing away from the audience: one of the singers turned him round so he could see the hall on its feet, clapping and waving hats.
l: You can create something great even when you lose the sense that seems essential.
q: Who turned Beethoven to face the audience at the Ninth's premiere?
A child in the front row

t: Why September, the ninth month, means “seven”
p: The oldest Roman calendar began in March. So September, October, November and December were the seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth months: septem, octo, novem, decem.
When, from 153 BC, the civil year began on 1 January, the names stayed, even though the numbers no longer added up.
l: Words keep traces of systems abandoned centuries ago.
q: Why is September named after the number seven?
The oldest Roman calendar began in March
It was the month of Rome's seventh king

t: We count time like the Babylonians
p: The sixty minutes in an hour and the 360 degrees in a circle come from the mathematics of Mesopotamia, which used base 60.
It is a handy number: it divides exactly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. Greek astronomers inherited it for angles and time, and we use it every time we look at a clock.
l: A practical system can outlive the civilisations that invented it by thousands of years.
q: Why did the Babylonians use base 60?
It divides exactly by many numbers
They counted sixty fingers and toes
It was the number of their gods

t: The day Italian women voted for the Republic
p: In the referendum of 2 June 1946 Italians chose between monarchy and republic: the republic won with about 54% of the vote.
It was also the first time women voted in a national election; 21 women were elected to the Constituent Assembly the same day. The Constitution it wrote came into force on 1 January 1948.
l: In Italy, the Republic and women's national vote share the same birthday.
q: How many women were elected to the Constituent Assembly in 1946?

t: Goldfish don't have a three-second memory
p: Experiments show that goldfish learn to press a lever for food, link sounds and colours to feeding time and remember it for weeks or months.
The three-second myth, repeated by adverts and films, has no scientific basis. On the other hand, a small bare bowl really is a terrible home for them.
l: “Truths” repeated by advertising need checking like everything else.
q: How long can a goldfish remember what it has learned?

t: You're taller in the morning than at night
p: During the day, standing or sitting, the discs between our vertebrae get squeezed and lose a little water: by evening we are about a centimetre shorter, sometimes more.
At night, lying down, the discs rehydrate. Astronauts in orbit, free from the weight of gravity, grow a few centimetres taller.
l: The body isn't a fixed measure: even your height changes during the day.
q: Why are we a little shorter in the evening?
The discs between the vertebrae get squeezed

t: Lightning does strike the same place twice
p: The proverb says otherwise, but lightning prefers high, pointed spots, and hits them again and again. New York's Empire State Building is struck about twenty times a year on average.
That's why lightning rods exist, invented by Benjamin Franklin in the mid-18th century.
l: A proverb can be reassuring and completely false.
q: About how many times a year is the Empire State Building struck?

t: First came the orange, then the colour orange
p: The fruit's name comes from the Sanskrit “nāraṅga”, which travelled through Persian and Arabic into Italian “arancia” and English “orange”.
The colour was named after the fruit, not the other way round: before oranges spread in Europe, many languages had no word of their own for it and called it “yellow-red”.
l: Many colour words come from concrete objects.
q: Which got its name first, the fruit or the colour orange?

t: The days of the week are seven heavenly bodies
p: In Italian, “lunedì” is the day of the Moon, “martedì” of Mars, “mercoledì” of Mercury, “giovedì” of Jupiter and “venerdì” of Venus. In Latin the last two days belonged to Saturn and the Sun too.
English kept them in Saturday and Sunday, and Monday is still the Moon's day. In Italian, Christianity turned them into “sabato”, from the Hebrew Shabbat, and “domenica”, the Lord's day.
l: Every time you say Monday or “lunedì”, you are quoting ancient astronomy.
q: Which heavenly body gives its name to “martedì”, Tuesday in Italian?

t: Do, re, mi come from a hymn to Saint John
p: Around 1025 the monk Guido of Arezzo taught singing with a hymn to Saint John the Baptist in which each line began one note higher: “Ut queant laxis, Resonare fibris, Mira gestorum…”.
The first syllables became the names of the notes. Later “ut” was replaced by “do”, which is easier to sing.
l: A good memory trick can become a system used for a thousand years.
q: Where do the note names do, re, mi come from?
The syllables of a hymn to Saint John

t: The world's most expensive violins come from Cremona
p: Antonio Stradivari worked in Cremona for over seventy years and made more than a thousand instruments; about 650 survive. One of his violins sold at auction for almost 16 million dollars.
The secret of their sound has been debated for centuries: wood, treatments, varnish. Yet in blind tests, soloists can't always tell them from the best modern violins.
l: An object's value also depends on the myth that surrounds it.
q: What have blind tests on Stradivari violins shown?
Soloists can't always tell them from the best modern violins
They always sound better than any other violin
Their secret is a honey varnish

t: Leonardo wrote backwards
p: In his notebooks Leonardo almost always wrote from right to left, with the letters reversed: you need a mirror to read them.

He was left-handed, and this way he probably avoided smudging the ink with his hand. About seven thousand pages of his notes survive, on anatomy, flying machines, water and painting, scattered across collections around the world.
l: A practical habit can become the unmistakable mark of a genius.
q: Why did Leonardo probably write backwards?
He was left-handed and avoided smudging the ink
He wanted to hide his secrets from the Church
